commentary.seminaVerbi:
Paul’s inversion of status is the psyche’s revolt against the false self: the persona built from pedigree, competence, and applause. What is “wise” and “mighty” is often just well-defended adaptation; what is “weak” is the unarmored core that can’t win by performance, so it must live by truth. The text presses a humiliating therapy: let the ego lose its favorite proofs, so life can be received rather than manufactured.

Mark stages the same dynamic as a court nightmare. Herod is split: he “hears willingly,” yet he cannot bear the social mirror of his guests. The banquet is a machine for turning private desire into public fate; the oath is not integrity but panic, a vow made to avoid looking small. Herodias is resentment with strategy; the girl is instrumentality dressed as charm; the platter is what happens when conscience is treated as an embarrassment to be removed.

Speculation: this resembles the Bhagavad Gita’s warning about attachment to honor and outcome, where action becomes bondage when it serves reputation. It echoes the Daoist preference for the low and uncarved, where power is exposed as brittle theater. It also touches Buddhist critiques of “conceit” (mana): the need to be someone at the table becomes the cause of harm. In Greek tragedy, especially Euripides’ Bacchae, the ruler who half-reveres the holy yet fears ridicule is dragged by spectacle into sacrilege. In Sufi adab, the real disgrace is not losing face but refusing the truth that would break the idol of the self.
commentary.excursus:
Paul’s “choice of the foolish” isn’t comfort; it’s a threat. It means the usual currencies—brains, pedigree, force—are being actively devalued, not politely ignored. The weak are not elevated because weakness is noble, but because weakness is usable. It slips past the guards of pride. It can be handled, directed, made into an instrument that humiliates the competent. “No flesh should glory” reads like a spiritual gag order: the self must be stripped of its right to narrate its own worth.

Herod’s banquet shows what happens when glory is the only religion. Power needs an audience, desire needs a stage, and an oath becomes a trap you set for yourself to look grand. Herod likes John because John is the one voice that doesn’t flatter him; the king listens “willingly” the way an addict listens to the dealer—fascinated by the very thing that condemns him. Herodias understands the psychology: you don’t defeat a prophet with arguments; you turn him into a platter.

The girl’s dance is not seduction as romance but seduction as mechanism. A body moves, a room agrees, and a man’s vanity signs a death warrant to avoid embarrassment. The head arrives like the real centerpiece of the feast: not food but proof that the king can still make reality obey him. Paul says the things that are “not” will bring to nothing the things that “are”; Mark shows the inverse dread, the ruler trying to erase the word that names his theft. He can kill the mouth, but the silence is louder, and the kingdom he offered “half” of is revealed as already hollow.
commentary.synthesis: God nullifies fleshly status by locating all righteousness in Christ. When power seeks legitimacy through spectacle and honor, it inevitably turns to blood to silence law.

gospel.text: Mark stages a chain of mediations: unlawful marriage produces imprisonment; resentment waits for occasion; a banquet supplies the mechanism; a mother scripts the request; disciples perform the only clean act—burial. The narrative is about how private sin recruits public institutions (prison, oath, execution) to silence a boundary-setting voice, and how the court’s pageantry cannot prevent its own moral collapse.

reading.text: Paul frames the community’s identity as a citation of Scripture: the only legitimate “glory” is doxological, because the community’s existence is derivative—“of him.” The argument is not anti-intellectual; it is anti-autonomous: any account of status that begins in “according to the flesh” is already a false genealogy.

marginalia.text: Vocation read sociologically: God’s call exposes the thinness of “wise…mighty…noble.”
Election as reversal: God chooses what the world uses as an insult.
“Things that are not”: ontological sabotage—nonbeing drafted to unmake being.
The target is boasting, not merely pride: flesh has no standing in court.
Christ is not a teacher of virtues but their substance: wisdom/justice/sanctification/redemption as one gift.
Prophetic speech is juridical: “not lawful” names a boundary, not an opinion.
Herod’s split mind: fear and fascination; conscience entertained as a hobby.
Power intoxicated by performance: a dance purchases a vow.
The oath is theater—“half my kingdom” from a petty king.
Honor culture as executioner: guests become the real tribunal.
The dish turns justice into cuisine; the head becomes a party favor.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: Lord our God, you willed that Saint John the Baptist should be the forerunner of the birth and the death of your Son; grant, through his intercession, that, as he died a martyr for truth and justice, we too may fight courageously for the confession of our faith. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God for ever and ever.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: Lord, blazing fire of eternal love, grant that, enkindled by your love, we may love you above all things and our neighbor for love of you. Through Jesus Christ our Lord.
hoursOfPrayer.label: Sext

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: Hear, Lord, our prayer and grant us the abundance of your peace, so that, through the intercession of Saint Mary, the Virgin, after having served you throughout our life, we may come before you without any fear. Through Jesus Christ our Lord.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer:
Let us pray:

After First Vespers of Sunday or of solemnities that fall on Sunday:

Keep us, Lord, through this night, and grant that tomorrow, as the new day dawns, the celebration of Sunday may fill us with the joy of the resurrection of your Son. Who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

After Vespers of solemnities that do not fall on Sunday:

Visit, Lord, this room; drive far from it the snares of the enemy. Let your holy angels dwell here and keep us in peace, and may your blessing remain always with us. Through Jesus Christ our Lord.

lines: For see your vocation, brethren, that there are not many wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble.
But the foolish things of the world hath God chosen, that he may confound the wise: and the weak things of the world hath God chosen, that he may confound the strong.
And the base things of the world and the things that are contemptible, hath God chosen: and things that are not, that he might bring to nought things that are:
That no flesh should glory in his sight.
But of him are you in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom and justice and sanctification and redemption:
That, as it is written: He that glorieth may glory in the Lord.

lines: For Herod himself had sent and apprehended John, and bound him prison for the sake of Herodias the wife of Philip his brother, because he had married her.
For John said to Herod: It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife.
Now Herodias laid snares for him: and was desirous to put him to death and could not.
For Herod feared John, knowing him to be a just and holy man: and kept him, and when he heard him, did many things: and he heard him willingly.
And when a convenient day was come, Herod made a supper for his birthday, for the princes, and tribunes, and chief men of Galilee.

And when the daughter of the same Herodias had come in, and had danced, and pleased Herod, and them that were at table with him, the king said to the damsel: Ask of me what thou wilt, and I will give it thee.
And he swore to her: Whatsoever thou shalt ask I will give thee, though it be the half of my kingdom.
Who when she was gone out, said to her mother, What shall I ask? But her mother said: The head of John the Baptist.
And when she was come in immediately with haste to the king, she asked, saying: I will that forthwith thou give me in a dish, the head of John the Baptist.
And the king was struck sad. Yet because of his oath, and because of them that were with him at table, he would not displease her:
But sending an executioner, he commanded that his head should be brought in a dish.
And he beheaded him in the prison, and brought his head in a dish: and gave to the damsel, and the damsel gave it her mother.
Which his disciples hearing came, and took his body, and laid it in a tomb.
